I almost lost my career as a Podiatrist to Plantar Fasciitis. Here's what saved me…

I've been a podiatrist for 21 years.

Last September, I almost had to close my practice…

Not because of money. Not because of a lawsuit.

… Because I couldn't stand up for more than 20 minutes without serious pain.

There were three mornings last summer when I sat on the edge of my bed and could not put my feet on the floor.

Not "didn't want to." Could not.

The pain was so bad I just sat there. A 51-year-old man. A doctor. Stuck on the side of his own bed because his feet hurt too much to stand up and go to work.

My wife found me on the second morning. She didn't say anything. She just got me a glass of water and sat next to me until I could make it to the bathroom.

That's when I knew I was in trouble.

Let me back up.

I'm a podiatrist. Foot doctor. I've been doing this since I was 30 years old. I see 30 patients a day. I'm on my feet for 9 hours. Concrete floor under thin carpet.

Plantar fasciitis is the most common thing I treat. I see it 15 times a day. I know every treatment. Every drug. Every procedure. I've done over 400 plantar fascia release surgeries in my career.

So when my own heel started hurting two years ago, I thought I had it handled.

I knew what to do. I'd been telling patients what to do for two decades.

I was wrong.

The pain started small. A little ache in my right heel in the morning. Gone by 10 AM. No big deal.

Six months later it was both feet. The morning pain lasted until lunch.

A year in, I was getting out of bed in stages. Sit up. Stretch the calf. Roll the foot on a frozen water bottle. Wait five minutes. Then stand.

My wife started bringing me coffee in bed. Not because she's sweet. Because I couldn't walk to the kitchen.

By month 14, I was lying to my staff.

I'd tell them I had a phone call so I could sit down in my office for ten minutes. I'd skip lunch and put my feet up instead of eating. I'd schedule my surgeries on Tuesdays so I could spend Monday and Wednesday in less pain.

My medical assistant noticed. She didn't say anything. But I saw her watching me.

I tried everything I tell my patients to try.

Cortisone injection. My partner did it. Felt better for five weeks. Then the pain came back worse. Every podiatrist knows cortisone weakens the fascia. We just don't tell patients because we have nothing better to offer.

Custom orthotics. $700. Molded to my feet. Wore them every day for four months. The pain didn't move.

Night splint. That big plastic boot that holds your foot at 90 degrees while you sleep. I lasted nine nights before I threw it across the bedroom.

Stretching. Twenty minutes every morning. Twenty minutes every night. For seven months. The first step out of bed still felt like stepping on a knife.

Ibuprofen. 800mg twice a day. My stomach started burning. My kidney labs started getting worse. My doctor told me to stop.

By month 16, I was sitting in my own exam room on a Saturday morning, looking at my own X-rays, and thinking about surgery.

Plantar fascia release. I've done 400 of them. I know the outcomes.

About 70% of patients get real relief. The other 30% develop arch collapse, side foot pain, or chronic instability that's worse than what they started with.

I wasn't going to gamble on 30%. Not on my own feet. Not when my career depended on it.

So I sat in that exam room and I made a decision.

I would close the practice.

I'd sell it to my partner. I'd take the buyout. I'd retire at 51 years old and figure out something else to do with my life. Something I could do sitting down.

I went home that Saturday and I didn't tell my wife. I couldn't say it out loud yet.

I just sat in the backyard and watched the sun go down.

Three days later, a patient walked into my exam room and changed everything.

Her name is Diane. She's an ER nurse. 58 years old. 30 years on her feet.

I'd been treating her plantar fasciitis for almost two years. We'd tried everything together. Cortisone twice. Orthotics. PT. Nothing worked for more than a few weeks.

She was one of my most frustrated patients.

She walked into my exam room that Tuesday morning and I noticed it before she even sat down.

She wasn't limping.

I asked her how her feet were doing.

She said, "Dr. Patel, I think I'm done with plantar fasciitis. I worked a 12-hour shift on Saturday and didn't even think about my feet."

I sat down on my rolling stool and just stared at her.

This was a woman who couldn't walk from her car to the ER doors six months ago without stopping.

"Diane. What did you do?"

She told me about a red light therapy wrap her daughter bought her. Said she let it sit on a shelf for a month because she'd "tried every gadget on Amazon" and didn't believe another one would work.

But her daughter kept asking, so she finally tried it.

"First week, my heel felt less angry," she said. "Week four, the morning pain was half. Week eight, I forgot to use it one night and only noticed the next morning because I didn't have to brace for the first step."

I'm going to be honest. I was skeptical.

After 21 years in podiatry, I've heard every miracle story. Copper socks. Magnetic insoles. Essential oils. Patients who swear something worked when really their pain was just in a low cycle.

But Diane wasn't that kind of patient. She was a charge nurse. She was as skeptical as I was. And I'd watched her struggle for two years.

And she wasn't limping.

Here's the thing though. I'd been seeing red light therapy everywhere lately.

NFL teams using it for recovery. UFC fighters. NBA training rooms. I'd read an article a few months back about how the longevity guys — Peter Attia, Andrew Huberman, those people — were all talking about it for inflammation and tissue repair.

I figured if pro athletes were spending real money on red light therapy for joint and tendon recovery, there had to be something to it. I just never thought about it for plantar fasciitis. I'd been trained that plantar fasciitis was a surgery problem. A cortisone problem. An orthotic problem.

It never crossed my mind that a wavelength of light could reach the fascia.

But Diane was standing there in my exam room and she wasn't limping.

That night, I got up at 2 AM to use the bathroom and my right heel locked up so badly I had to sit on the toilet for four minutes before I could walk back to bed.

I sat there in the dark, in pain, on my own toilet, and I thought about Diane walking into my office that morning.

I started researching.

Turns out, the science on red light therapy and plantar fasciitis is real. Really real.

There's a study from BMJ Open — that's a peer-reviewed medical journal — with 18 randomized trials, 784 patients, 11 of those trials specifically on plantar fasciitis. Red light therapy showed clear pain reduction. No side effects. The studies using the right doses outperformed placebo by a lot.

Not fringe. Not pseudoscience. Real clinical research.

I'd been a podiatrist for 21 years and I'd never seriously studied this. None of us do. We're trained in surgery, drugs, and orthotics. That's it.

But then I noticed something in the research that stopped me cold.

The studies that failed had a pattern.

Wrong wavelength. Wrong power. Wrong treatment time.

The studies that worked used very specific settings: 660nm red light AND 850nm near-infrared. Both wavelengths. Together. At therapeutic power. For 15 to 20 minutes per session.

That's the problem with the red light therapy market right now.

Most products either claim to use both wavelengths but don't actually deliver them. Or they only use one — usually just 660nm. Or the power output is so weak it doesn't matter what wavelength they're using.

There's a lot of garbage out there.

Your plantar fascia sits 3 to 4 millimeters below your heel pad. To reach that tissue, you need 850nm near-infrared light. That's the only wavelength that goes deep enough.

But most consumer wraps don't even list their power output. The label just says "red light therapy." That's it. No numbers. No wavelengths. Just a vague promise.

So you're buying what you think is therapy, but you're really getting a flashlight pressed against your foot.

I tried two anyway.

First one was $49. Used it every night for five weeks. My morning pain didn't budge.

Second one was $89. Six weeks. Same result.

I was running out of time.

I'd already told my partner we needed to talk about the practice. I had three weeks before the conversation I couldn't take back.

So I went back to what Diane said. She'd been specific. She said most red light wraps didn't work — but this one did. She showed me the box in my exam room.

FootRevive.

I looked it up expecting to be disappointed again.

But it was different.

Dual wavelength. 660nm red AND 850nm near-infrared. The exact combination from the clinical studies.

Therapeutic power density printed right on the spec sheet.

Designed to wrap around the heel and arch. The two places where 95% of plantar fasciitis pain comes from.

Not a generic foot pad. A wrap shaped for the actual anatomy of the plantar fascia.

I ordered it that night. I didn't tell my wife. I didn't tell my partner. I had three weeks before I had to make a decision about my career.

It arrived four days later.

I used it that night on the couch after a 9-hour day. Wrapped it around my heel. Set the timer for 20 minutes.

About ten minutes in, I noticed something.

The deep ache I always had in my heel by the end of the day — the dull throbbing I'd lived with for so long I'd forgotten what its absence felt like — was just quieter.

Not gone. Quieter.

The next morning I got out of bed and took my first step.

Still hurt. But it was a 5 out of 10 instead of a 7.

I stood there in my bedroom and I just stared at the floor for a minute.

A 5 was the best morning I'd had in 14 months.

Week two: first step was a 4. I walked to the bathroom without limping for the first time in over a year.

Week four: I forgot to use it one Thursday because I fell asleep on the couch. Friday morning was worse than Wednesday. That's when I knew it was actually working. The absence created a measurable change.

Week six: I worked a full clinic day, came home, and went for a 20-minute walk with my wife after dinner. We hadn't taken an evening walk together in over a year. She didn't say anything during the walk. When we got home, she put her hand on my back and her hand was shaking.

She'd noticed everything I thought I'd been hiding. Every wince. Every excuse. Every morning I sat on the edge of the bed too long.

She'd been watching me disappear and she didn't know how to say it.

Week eight: I got out of bed at 5:45 AM, walked straight to the bathroom, made coffee, and was halfway through reading the news before I realized I hadn't done my morning warmup.

I hadn't needed to.

I stood in my kitchen holding the coffee mug and I just laughed. Out loud. By myself. In my own kitchen at 6 AM.

My wife came downstairs and asked what was so funny.

I told her, "Nothing hurts."

She didn't say anything. She just put her arms around me and held on.

I went into the office that morning and I pulled up the meeting I'd scheduled with my partner.

I cancelled it.

I didn't tell him why for another month.

When Diane came back for her six-month follow-up, I told her everything.

How close I'd come to closing the practice. How I'd been sitting on the edge of my bed in the mornings unable to stand up. How her offhand comment about red light therapy had probably saved my career.

She just smiled and said, "Dr. Patel. You've been treating my feet for two years. I'm just glad I got to do something for you."

That was four months ago.

My morning pain this week? A 0 or 1. Some mornings I feel nothing at all.

No surgery. No cortisone weakening my fascia. No $700 orthotics. No night splint. No ibuprofen eating my stomach. No selling my practice. No retiring at 51.

No watching my career disappear because my feet decided to quit before I was ready.

Last weekend my daughter asked me to hike with her. A real hike. Five miles. Elevation.

Two years ago I would have said no and made up a reason. I'd been quietly saying no to her for almost a year because I knew what my feet would feel like the next morning.

I said yes.

I did the whole hike. She kept looking at me like she was waiting for me to ask to turn back. I didn't.

The next morning I got out of bed and walked to the kitchen and made coffee. No warmup. No stretching. No limping.

Just walking. Like a person whose feet work.

I'm sharing this because I think you might be where I was eight months ago.

Turns out I DON'T have plantar fasciitis. And if your first step still hurts, you might not either. A circulation doctor showed me what's actually tearing it open every morning.

For almost my entire life, I was a runner.

Not casually either. Thirty to forty miles a week since my twenties. I'm 45 now.

The rest of my life looks like this. I sit at a desk for nine hours, I come home, and I run. That's been the shape of my days for close to twenty years.

I never thought about my feet because they never gave me a reason to.

Then one morning I stood up out of bed and my right heel felt like I'd stepped on broken glass.

That was the beginning of two and a half years.

I'm going to tell you everything I tried, in order.

Here's what the first six months looked like.

The pain showed up after runs. Then during runs. Then it stopped waiting for runs at all and just lived there.

And it went past stepping on broken glass.

It became a nail driven into my heel, or a Lego brick pressed into it, all day long.

I tried explaining it to people. Nobody ever really understood.

By month four I couldn't walk to the mailbox without limping the first twenty steps.

So I did what everyone tells you to do first.

I stopped running. Completely. Not reduced. Stopped.

Six weeks of nothing.

I never really got back to running after that. A mile here and there, always paid for the next morning.

And here's the first thing that confused me. The rest didn't help.

It got slightly better for about four days, then it plateaued, and by week five it was getting worse while I was doing absolutely nothing.

It made no sense to me, and it kept making no sense for two years.

Then I started testing everything else, one at a time, because if you change five things at once you learn nothing.

I started with the shoes, because that's what everyone says.

Eight pairs. Every one of them followed the same pattern. The first two hours felt better and I'd think, this is the one. Then the afternoon came, and the pain punched right through the cushioning.

Then the custom orthotics. Three hundred dollars, molded to my arch.

Same result, more expensive. They worked right up until I took them off at the door. Then the first step inside split my heel open again.

Then stretching, because half the internet is convinced tight calves are the whole story.

Every morning and every night. The wall stretch, the towel pull, calf raises off the bottom stair. My calves got looser. I could reach further than I had in years.

My heel didn't notice. Three weeks, no change. Six weeks, no change. Ten weeks, no change.

Then the massage gun, every night, on those same calves.

Twenty minutes a night for months. It felt good while I did it. My calves felt worked on, looser, warmer. And the next morning my heel greeted me exactly the same way it always did.

The frozen water bottle. Every night until my heel went numb.

The cold quieted the burning while the cold was there. Twenty minutes after I dried my foot off, the stabbing came back, angrier for having been interrupted.

The night splint. Eight hours of my foot held stretched.

I gave the whole thing back in one second, on the first step of the morning.

Cortisone. Twice, at the clinical dose.

Quiet for a few weeks, then the slow return, and the appointment for the next one already in my calendar.

Two podiatrists. One ultrasound that showed thickening, which sounded serious and told me nothing about what to actually do.

Some of it helped for a day or two.

Then that pain always came back.

Two and a half years of that.

At some point I stopped believing any of it was going to work.

And one night I found myself thinking back through the whole two and a half years, everything I'd done, trying to find any pattern at all.

Three things didn't fit the story I'd been told.

One. Six weeks of complete rest made it worse. Not neutral. Worse.

Two. There were days I was on my feet constantly, running errands all afternoon, and I woke up the next morning better than usual. I never understood why.

Three. Every single thing that ever helped, only helped for a while. The ice. The stretching. Even the shot.

Not one of them ever lasted.

Everything I'd been told said rest heals it and load damages it.

My own two and a half years said something else entirely.

That's when I stopped researching plantar fasciitis and started researching why a heel might not heal.

And somewhere down in a thread, I found a comment from a woman who said her heel finally healed once she fixed her circulation.

Her circulation.

Two and a half years of reading. Stretches, shoes, insoles, splints, shots. Every single thing pointed at the foot.

This was the first thing I had ever read that pointed somewhere else.

I booked an appointment with a circulation doctor. A real physician who specializes in it. Not another foot doctor.

She let me talk all the way through without interrupting.

I told her all of it. The two and a half years. Everything I'd tried. And the part that had never made sense to me. That I rested it completely for six weeks, and it got worse.

She nodded.

"That's not strange. That's actually the answer."

Then she pulled over a notepad and drew a foot, and a line running up the back of the leg.

"Here's what nobody explained to you. The bottom of your foot is just about the hardest place in your whole body for blood to reach. It's the farthest point from your heart. And it's the one place where blood has to climb straight back up, against GRAVITY, to get out."

"Okay," I said.

"What makes that climb happen is a muscle deep in your calf. It's called the soleus. Some people call it the second heart. Every time it squeezes, it pushes the blood out of your feet and back up your legs."

"My calf? But the pain is in my heel."

"Stay with me. How many hours a day are you at that desk?"

"Nine."

"For how many years?"

"Close to twenty."

"That's what stacked up. That muscle stiffens the longer it spends not moving, and it does it a little more every year. By the time you hit your forties, yours had been stiffening long enough to stop."

"Once it stiffens, it can't push the blood back up anymore. So the old blood just sits down there in your foot. Pooling. Going nowhere. We call it stagnant blood."

"And as long as that old blood is sitting there, fresh blood can't get in behind it. It can't reach your heel at all."

"So it was never the plantar fascia."

"Think about what that means," she said. "Every step you take opens tiny damage in your heel. That's normal. That's just what walking is. In most people, it heals overnight."

"Mine doesn't."

"Healing takes oxygen. Oxygen rides in on fresh blood. And fresh blood isn't reaching your heel. So this morning, your first step came down on damage that never healed. And tore it open again."

She let that sit there a second.

"Torn open. Never healed. Torn open again. Every morning. That's the stabbing."

"So the running was making it worse."

"You were opening more damage than most people ever do, with less ability to heal it than most people have. That's the whole picture."

"Then why didn't running fix the muscle? I did it for twenty years."

"Because by the time this started, it was already too stiff for that. Once it's there, normal movement isn't enough to bring it back. That's the point you were already past."

"And the six weeks of rest?"

"You added six more weeks of not moving to a muscle that was already stiffening from exactly that. You weren't resting it. You were speeding it up."

I want you to understand what that did to me, sitting in that chair.

Two and a half years of doing exactly what I was told, and the thing I'd been told was the single most damaging thing I did.

"Then why didn't the massage gun work? I've been on those calves every night for two years."

"On the surface," she said. "The muscle you can reach with a massage gun or a stretch is the one on top. The soleus sits underneath it. You can't get to it by pressing from the outside. It has to contract."

Then I said the thing I'd been holding since I sat down.

"I've spent thousands of dollars on shoes and insoles."

"Every insole you've ever bought sits under your foot," she said. "The reason your heel can't heal is above it."

I sat there going back through everything I'd tried.

Every single thing on that list was aimed at the part that hurt. Not one of them had ever gone anywhere near the reason the blood stopped reaching my heel in the first place.

I asked her how to get it working again.

"You have to make it squeeze. Directly. In the clinic we use EMS for that. Electrical stimulation, at a frequency that goes deep enough to reach the soleus. It makes the muscle contract on its own, without you standing, without you moving."

"The contractions loosen it, and the pump starts working again. The stagnant blood finally moves out, fresh blood gets in, and the damage in your heel starts getting the oxygen it needs. It starts healing for the first time in years."

"Do I have to keep coming here?"

"There are home units now. But listen, because this part matters. If it doesn't run at 40Hz, it's not reaching the soleus. It's just buzzing your skin. Most of what's out there is a massager with a fancy name. Check the frequency before you buy anything."

That night I sat at the kitchen table with my phone.

She was right. Page after page of foot massagers. Soothing vibration. Relaxing relief. Not one of them said what frequency they ran at.

Then I found one that did. A flat mat called FlowLab Revive. Right on the page: 40Hz EMS, built to reach the soleus. You sit in a chair, put your bare feet on it, fifteen minutes.

It had a 90-day money-back guarantee.

After everything that hadn't worked, one more try wasn't going to break me.

I was diagnosed with plantar fasciitis at 46. I'm 51 now. Turns out that was never what was wrong with my feet.

For five years I "managed" a diagnosis that was only ever half the story.

At 46 I was hiking most weekends and walking with my husband every evening after dinner. By 47 my whole life had shrunk to whatever my feet would allow that day, and the doctors kept telling me the feet were the whole problem.

Five years of stretching my calves against the doorframe before I was allowed to take a step. Five years of rolling a frozen water bottle under my foot every night for ten minutes of relief that was gone by the time I stood up. I did everything they asked.

I bought the Hokas, then the Brooks, then Birkenstocks, then Oofos slides for the house, then a pair of Vionics. After the shoes came the Dr. Scholl's inserts, then Superfeet, then a night splint, then the Strassburg sock.

I paid $500 for custom orthotics that insurance wouldn't cover, because the podiatrist swore they'd fix it in a month. Within two weeks they'd given me nerve pain in both feet every time I put them on.

The cortisone shot helped for about four weeks, and I wore sandals on holiday like a normal person. Then it wore off, and it took the sandals with it.

Then they sent me to a specialist. Podiatrist first, then an orthopedic surgeon, then a rheumatologist, eight months of appointments in all.

The X-rays were clean. The ultrasound showed the band under my heel was thickened, which they said just confirmed the diagnosis, and the blood work for rheumatoid arthritis and thyroid came back normal.

"Everything looks fine," the surgeon said. "It's plantar fasciitis. It's common at this age, and we've ruled out everything else."

I felt like I was making it up. The tests were clean and the doctors weren't worried, and every single morning my feet refused to hold me up without pain.

By the time my alarm went off at 5:40, I already knew what the first step was going to feel like. I'd swing my legs over the side and put my hand flat on the wall before my foot touched the floor. That first step felt like someone had caned my feet in the night.

By 10am I'd be standing at the front desk of the vet clinic where I work, concrete floor, first two Advil down. Still nothing.

By 2pm the bottoms of my feet were the worst part of me. It felt like walking on marbles, like there was nothing between my bones and the concrete.

And the math never stopped. If I walked the dog to the end of the street and back, I was done for the night.

I stopped walking anywhere I didn't have to, and took up the exercise bike in the garage instead, and put on thirty pounds because I couldn't walk more than a mile.

My husband still went out for his walk every evening after dinner. I watched him go from the couch, same spot, and two years earlier we'd climbed a mountain on our anniversary and now I could hardly climb the stairs to bed.

I'd told him to stop asking me to come. When he stopped asking, that was worse.

Last spring I went on vacation with my parents, who are almost 80, and they zoomed around the whole week while I kept taking breaks for my feet. On the day everyone hiked out to the waterfall, I stayed at the hotel.

I wanted to be out with the dog, cooking, even cleaning the house. Instead I was on the couch, because even standing hurt, and I hadn't seen my friends in months because everything they did involved walking.

I looked fine on the outside. Inside, every part of my life was getting smaller, and my feet were the reason for all of it.

And every doctor just nodded. "That's plantar fasciitis. It's an age thing, and losing a few pounds would help."

I tried losing the pounds, and it cost me two weeks of worse pain. When my hips started aching too I got the HRT patch, and it took the hip ache and the hot flashes and left my feet exactly where they were.

After that came the walking boot, the Epsom soaks, the acupuncture. Nothing worked, and every season there was one more thing I didn't do anymore.

I started to believe this was just my life now. That I'd spend the rest of it watching everyone else go while I planned my whole day around my feet. It felt like the next step was crutches, and after that my life was basically over.

Then my neighbor asked me a question no podiatrist ever had. She's a nurse at a foot and ankle clinic. We were standing in her driveway and I was telling her I couldn't get through the grocery store anymore without sitting in the car for twenty minutes after, and that I'd just cancelled the hiking trip we'd booked a year ago.

"Has anyone ever actually pressed on your heel and checked how much padding is left under it?"

I almost laughed. "I've tried insoles and I've tried orthotics, and they didn't do anything."

She shook her head. "That's not what I asked. Press your thumb into the middle of your heel."

I did, standing there in her driveway, and it was bone, right under the skin.

"Ten years ago there was a thick pad of fat there," she said. "It's your body's shock absorber. Every step you've ever taken landed on it."

"You're telling me I'm missing fat off the bottom of my feet?"

"I'm telling you that plantar fasciitis was never the real problem. It's what happens when the pad goes."

"Your heel bone hits the floor about 8,000 times a day. With the pad there, that gets spread out. With the pad gone, all of it lands on one hard point, and that hammering is what keeps the band under your heel inflamed."

"Overnight it starts to heal. Then your first step in the morning lands bone on floor and rips it open again. That's why you hold the wall."

"What would even cause that?"

"It thins as your hormones shift. From your mid-30s on, and women's pads are thinner than men's to begin with. Your weight didn't do this, and neither did your shoes."

She looked at me. "Your life didn't get smaller because there's anything wrong with you. One part wore out, and nobody warned you."

"Once it's gone, it doesn't grow back. Researchers call it fat pad atrophy, and it keeps your heel landing on bone even on the days you rest it, even after the stretches, even when the X-ray comes back clean."

"The band was sore because the bone was hammering it. You've spent five years treating the sore part and nothing under it."

"That first step in the morning, after a full night of sleep? That's not plantar fasciitis. That's your heel bone hitting the floor with nothing between them."

"And the marbles feeling?"

"Same thing. Pain is weight on a small spot, and comfort is the same weight spread over a big area. You can lie on a bed of nails, but you can't lie on one nail."

"But I've tried insoles," I said.

"You tried half the job," she said. "A fix has to do two jobs at once: put a real pad between the bone and the floor, and spread your weight across the whole foot so the bone doesn't carry it all. Everything you bought did one or the other."

"Drugstore inserts are the soft part, badly. A few millimetres of foam, and your bare heel squashes it flat on the first step. Your custom orthotics were the spreading part, hard plastic straight under a bare bone, which is why they hurt."

"Half the job feels like nothing."

I stared at her. Five years, three specialists, every test coming back clean, and nobody had ever pressed on my heel.

I went home and Googled "heel fat pad thinning women" and fell into a rabbit hole. Foot and ankle journals describing the pad under the heel thinning with age and hormone changes.

Everything she said checked out.

I texted her the next morning. "Okay, say you're right. What do I actually do?"

She called on her lunch break. "The pad doesn't grow back, so you put one under your foot from the outside. You need two parts in one insole."

"A thick pad under the heel and the front of the foot, thick enough that a bare heel can't flatten it. And a firm cradle under the arch that catches part of every step, so the heel never carries the whole load alone."

"Soft where you're bare, firm where you're not. Your heel stops hammering, and the band finally gets a rest that lasts past the first step."

"And it has to go in the slippers by your bed. The first step of the day is the one that does the damage, and your Hokas are by the front door at 5:40 in the morning."

"I keep a pair in my own slippers. We started telling patients about them last year."

This sounded too simple to me. But I'd been dragging myself through every day for five years. "Where do I get one?"

"You can't grab any insole off the shelf," she said. "Most of them are either thin foam or a hard shell, and the thick ones flatten out in a month."

"The one I use is Rebloom. It's a thick foam base under the heel and the front of the foot, with a firm arch cradle built into it, and you trim it to fit. It's the only one I've found that does both."

I looked it up that night. There was a 90-day money-back guarantee. After five years of shoes and shots and specialists that failed, what was one more try?

They came in four days, and I put them straight into the slippers by my bed. The first morning I still put my hand on the wall out of habit, and the step still hurt. Like ten percent less.

By day four, I got to the bathroom without touching the wall, and stood there with my hand up in the air where the wall should have been.

By the end of week one I moved them into my work sneakers and got through a full shift on that concrete without my afternoon Advil. I'd forgotten to take it.

Since spring I'd been keeping a list on my phone of how far I could walk before my feet quit. By the end of week two, it was around the block twice with no sitting in between. Nearly triple what I'd managed all year.

Then came week three. I woke up before my alarm, lay in the quiet, and waited for it. The caned feeling, the marbles, that first-step pain that had met me every single morning for five years.

It wasn't there. I put my foot down and it held, and for the first time in five years the word for it wasn't "manageable." It was fine.

For the first time in five years, I walked barefoot across my kitchen tile to make coffee and didn't think about my feet until the coffee was done.

That Saturday I walked the dog to the end of the street and back and kept going, and got through the whole day without planning it around my feet.

For the first time in five years, my husband put his shoes on for his walk and I put mine on too. Halfway around the block he looked at me and said "you're walking like yourself again."

Two weekends later I did the trail behind the reservoir, the one I hadn't touched in four years. Three miles, and I sat in the car afterward and cried, and for once it wasn't from pain.

Five years of trails and evening walks and trips I sat out, and the whole time it was never my life that had to get smaller. It was a pad.

I don't have a plantar fasciitis problem. I never did. And my life was never over, either.

What I'd had was five years of a missing pad, my heel hitting the floor with nothing between them, and a sore band taking the blame.

And not one person in a white coat thought to press on my heel.

I still wear the patch, and I still do the stretches out of habit. The concrete at work hasn't changed either. But now there's a pad under my heel before my foot touches the floor.

Every morning my feet go straight into the slippers with the pad in them, and at work they go into my sneakers. There's nothing to take and nothing to do, and it takes as long as putting on shoes.

That should be the first thing anyone tells a woman whose feet started hurting in her 40s.

If you've been told you have plantar fasciitis… If you've done the stretches and the shots and the orthotics and nothing has stuck…

If your X-rays and your blood work keep coming back clean… If you wake up after eight hours of sleep and put your hand on the wall before your foot touches the floor…

If you've stopped saying yes to the walk, the market, the vacation… If your world has shrunk to whatever your feet will allow that day…

I'm not saying you're definitely missing the pad under your heel. But I spent five years treating a sore band while the real problem got worse every single day, and five years watching my life get smaller every season over one part that had simply worn out.

Rebloom is a small company that makes one thing.

Right now they're running a sale. I checked the site this morning and ordered a second pair, so I can stop moving one pair back and forth between the slippers and my work shoes.

They have a 90-day money-back guarantee. Three full months to find out if it works for you. If nothing changes, you get your money back.

But if it works? If the first morning that step lands on padding instead of bone, even just a little?

If by week one you get to the bathroom without touching the wall? If a month from now you put your shoes on for the evening walk and go the whole way, and the weekend after that you're back on a trail?

You'll wish you'd started five years ago. I know I do. I took all of it for granted.

I've done every level of my physical therapy program. I've been stuck at the top for four months. My PT said there's nothing left to try but a shot. Then I found out a woman in the same waiting room was improving every week on a THIRD of my exercises. Now I know why.

There's a moment I want to tell you about, because if you're anywhere near the top of your PT program for plantar fasciitis, you're headed toward it.

It's the moment your physical therapist runs out of program.

I'm 56. Fourteen months of PT for my left heel. And four months ago, at my re-evaluation, my physical therapist looked at my chart, looked at me, and said the sentence I'd been dreading since around month six.

"Lisa, you're at the top of the program. You've plateaued. There's nothing left for me to add."

And then, because she's kind, she offered me the consolation prize.

"I can send a note to your podiatrist about a cortisone shot. And if that doesn't hold, he might want to talk about a surgical consult."

A shot. Then maybe surgery. Fourteen months in. Or accept where I was.

Let me back up, because I know that program. I climbed every level of it.

I started fourteen months ago. Level one was towel stretches and rolling a frozen water bottle. Six good weeks. My first step went from a 9 to a 7. Then it slowed, and we moved up.

Level two: calf raises on the floor, three sets of fifteen. That bought me a few more good weeks. Then it slowed. We moved up.

And that became the shape of my whole year. Every level up bought me a few weeks of progress and a lot of soreness. Then the progress would slow, then stop, and we'd move up again. Each level bought a little less than the one before.

Calf raises on a step. Then single-leg. Then single-leg with a backpack full of books. Then three sessions of shockwave therapy at $300 each.

My first step went from a 9 to a 5. I'm not ungrateful for that. But a 5 is still a stab every morning. And I'm a pharmacy tech. I stand nine hours a day. My job is counting on getting the rest of the way there.

And at the top of the program, the pattern I'd been outrunning for a year finally caught me.

Four months. The hardest level. Nothing.

And here's what the top level actually felt like, since nobody talks about it.

The pain wasn't even steady. That's the part that made me feel crazy. On the hardest, most advanced program, a quiet week was okay. But a hard week, a double shift, my mother's move into assisted living, and the nail came straight back. Me, at the top of my PT program, standing at the pharmacy counter at 4 PM shifting from foot to foot, unable to stand still.

Like stress and long days had a manual override on the strongest program there is.

My podiatrist took X-rays. No heel spur. No fracture. My PT measured everything. My ankle flexibility was "great." My calf strength was "excellent for your age."

Everything came back fine.

So I posted in my plantar fasciitis group. Top of the PT program, four months stuck, PT says nothing left. And I got forty answers.

"Get the shot. Mine lasted six months." And for some women it does. But other women in that group got the shot, felt great for six weeks, and were back worse than before. Nobody talks about them.

"Try PRP injections." $1,200, not covered.

"Some feet just don't fully heal. A 5 is a win."

"Lose weight, it takes pressure off." I'd already lost 18 pounds since this started, eating salads at my desk.

And then the one I still think about.

"Honestly, if the hardest PT isn't working, it's not the PT anymore. It's just your feet."

I read that one in the break room and just sat there. Because that's the thing about the top of the program. On every other level, there was somewhere to put the blame. The exercises were too easy. Now there was nowhere left. If the hardest program doesn't work on you, you're not under-treated anymore. You're broken.

That's what "nothing left to try" means when you take it home. It doesn't mean the PT ran out. It means you did.

And here's the part nobody could explain.

My next-morning soreness got worse every time we added weight. By the top level, the morning after a PT session was the worst first step of my week. Every time. My heel was screaming that something was wrong, while every test said I was fine.

On the strongest program. Hurting the most after it. Nobody found that strange but me.

Meanwhile my group was a highlight reel. "Back to running!" "Pain-free in 8 weeks!" And the ones who'd plateaued, quietly getting the shot, disappearing from the group for a few months, and coming back with a boot and the same story.

One night at 1 AM I googled "plateaued in PT plantar fasciitis."

Reddit threads. "Chronic plantar fasciitis" articles. "Some people never fully recover" pieces. And the surgery forums, full of people on their second and third procedures. I read it all with my heart pounding and thought, that's my future.

I drafted the email to my podiatrist asking for the shot. It sat in my drafts. Unsent. Because something about it felt like admitting the problem was never going to be fixed, just numbed.

Then I asked a stranger the question that changed everything.

There was a woman in my PT's waiting room, I'll call her Gina, who came in on Tuesdays like me. We'd started chatting. Same heel problem. Started PT around the same time. I'd watched her through the glass. She was doing a third of my program. Floor calf raises, a few stretches, a walk on the treadmill. And every week she was telling the front desk she was better than the week before.

I'd been quietly furious at her for two months, if I'm being honest.

One Tuesday I just asked.

"Can I ask you something? How are you still getting better on that program? I'm doing three times as much and I've been stuck since spring."

She smiled a little.

"You're going to be mad."

"Why would I be mad?"

"Because it's something my PT made me start before my very first session. It's about $35 a month. And I figured every PT did that, until I talked to you."

Before Gina's first appointment, her physical therapist, at a different clinic before she moved here, told her something she'd written in her phone. She showed me.

"Every patient I put on loading starts collagen with vitamin C first, an hour before every session. Because the exercises are about to create a demand for new tissue that their body can't meet. And the harder we push the load, the bigger the bill."

I read it twice. Then I said:

"Collagen? I TAKE collagen."

Every night. Since month three. The big tub from Target, a scoop in my tea before bed. It was on my kitchen counter right now.

"What kind?" she asked.

The kind with a woman's face on the label. I had no idea.

"That's the problem. Wrong kind, and wrong time. Let me explain it the way she explained it to me. Because it explains your whole program."

So here it is, the way Gina gave it to me in a PT waiting room, from a woman doing a third of my exercises.

Your plantar fascia is a band of tissue made almost entirely of one material: type I collagen. When you have chronic heel pain, that tissue isn't mostly inflamed. It's worn. Frayed, tangled collagen that's been patched over with weak material.

PT is how you rebuild it. Every time you load the tissue with calf raises, steps, walking, you're telling it: break down the weak stuff and rebuild stronger.

But rebuilding takes material. New collagen has to be built out of something. And your body needs vitamin C to build it at all. Without vitamin C, it can't link the fibers into strong tissue.

The exercises are the order. The collagen and vitamin C are the delivery.

Now here's the trap, and fourteen months of appointments never once covered it.

Most women over 50 are already making a lot less collagen than they used to. Your body's own production drops every year after your mid-twenties, and menopause drops it hard.

Then you start PT, and the exercises do exactly what they're supposed to. They ask your heel to rebuild.

And at the same time, half of us get told to lose weight. So we eat less. Less protein. Fewer of the foods that give your body building blocks.

More orders. Fewer deliveries.

"Now look at your program," Gina said. "Every time your PT raised the load, she asked your heel to rebuild more than the level before. Same short supply. Bigger bill. The level that's supposed to be the strongest is the level where you're asking your body for the most it's ever had to build, with the least it's ever had to build with."

"That's why each level bought you less than the one before. The program got harder and your supply got thinner at the same time. And that's why I'm still improving on my easy program. My exercises are lighter. But my body has what it needs to answer them."

"The program was never measuring the exercises. It was measuring the supply."

I sat with that for a long time. Fourteen months of PT rearranged themselves in my head. Every level: a little progress, then the stall, then up. It was never my heel finding its limit. It was the supply running out a little faster each time.

And the next-morning soreness. "That's why it got worse every level," Gina said. "Her words, not mine. She said the patients at the top of the program hurt the worst the day after, and they always get told they're overdoing it."

I pushed back. Obviously. I'd earned my skepticism at $40 a copay.

"My PT tested everything. My flexibility and strength are great."

"She tested what PT tests. Flexibility. Strength. Range of motion. Nobody tests how fast your heel is actually rebuilding. Nobody can, in a clinic. So everything they can measure comes back fine."

Everything they measured was fine. The thing that wasn't fine, nobody could measure. They had a sentence for me instead. You've plateaued. And a sentence is where the investigating stops.

"This sounds like the collagen girls on Instagram," I said. "The glowing-skin videos. If a scoop of powder fixed heels, we'd all be fixed."

"I said the exact same thing to her," Gina said. "And she said, I'm not selling you glowing skin. Your PT is asking your heel to rebuild. Building takes material. If you don't supply the material, the program stalls. That's not a trend. That's arithmetic. And you're on the hardest program, so for you it's more arithmetic, not less."

"But I've been taking collagen this whole time."

"Wrong kind, wrong time. The beauty tubs are a blend of types I and III, dosed for skin, with no vitamin C. And you take it at bedtime, ten hours before you use your foot. The study she showed me gave people collagen with vitamin C an hour before a few minutes of exercise, and the marker for new collagen production roughly doubled. The materials have to be in your blood when the tissue gets worked."

She pulled up a photo on her phone. A white tub.

Fascora.

"This is the one she told me to get. Ten grams of type I collagen in a scoop. That's the kind your heel is made of. 100 milligrams of vitamin C in the same scoop. Boswellia and curcumin so the soreness after PT doesn't stop you. MSM. Every amount right on the label."

"One scoop in your coffee an hour before PT. On the other days, an hour before a ten-minute walk. That's it."

That was the whole protocol. That was the thing I'd be mad about.

Fourteen months. Every level of the program. Thousands of dollars in copays and shockwave. A physical therapist telling me there was nothing left to add. And a woman doing a third of my exercises had been given the answer before her first session.

I still half didn't believe her, so here's what I did next.

I went home and read for three hours. The research on chronic plantar fasciitis tissue under a microscope: degenerated, not inflamed. The collagen and vitamin C before exercise study. The Danish study showing that loading helps plantar fasciitis more than stretching alone. I read my own PT's exercise sheets differently now. Every one was asking my heel to build something.

It all checked out. I'd scrolled past collagen ads for months assuming they were for desperate women like me. Some of them are. The arithmetic isn't.

I ordered that night.

60-day money-back guarantee. I'd just been offered "a cortisone shot and maybe surgery" as my best option. A tub of collagen was not the risk in my life.

Day one, nothing. I want to be honest about that.

End of week one, the morning after PT wasn't the worst morning of my week anymore. The soreness I used to carry until noon was gone by the time I got to work.

Week two is when it happened.

I got out of bed on a Wednesday, the morning after a PT session, and my first step was a 3. Not a 5. A 3. And at my Tuesday session that week, for the first time in four months, my PT wrote in my chart that I'd progressed.

Same program. Same exercises. The exact level she'd looked at and said there was nothing left to add.

And here's the part I need to be precise about, because it matters.

Nothing about my PT changed. Same program. Same level. Same exercises she'd called "done."

There was never anything wrong with the program. My body finally had the material to answer it.

Weeks three and four, steady. A good morning, then a better one. The way level one had felt fourteen months ago, except this time it didn't stall. Then Thanksgiving hit. I cooked for fourteen people and stood in my kitchen from 7 AM to 9 PM. For the first time in two years, the next morning was fine. That's when I actually believed it.

Day 26, the tub was almost empty. I put on the hiking boots I haven't worn in two years and walked the trail behind our neighborhood with my husband. Two miles. My first step the next morning was a 2.

That was one tub.

Gina's still on her easy program, still improving. We sit together on Tuesdays now.

For four months I thought I'd gotten everything PT had to give. That the hardest level had measured me and found the limit, and the limit was mine.

The program never measured me. Every level up asked my heel to build more, and I was eating less, and taking the wrong collagen at the wrong time. By the top of the program, I was asking my body for the most it had ever built, with the least it had ever had to build with. PT didn't run out at the top. The material did.

I'm going to say something that nobody with plantar fasciitis wants to hear, and I honestly don't care if it upsets you.

Cortisone is not going to fix your heel.

Not the shot. Not the $450 orthotics. Not the night splint. Not the Hokas everyone in your Facebook group swears by.

None of it is going to fix this.

I know because I tried all of it. Every shot. Every insert. Every shoe. For three years. And it got so bad my podiatrist started using the word "surgery." Because I spent three years numbing and propping up a problem nobody ever bothered to explain to me.

And the worst part? My daughter started limping the exact same way. Same feet. Same job on her feet. Same first step out of bed.

And I almost let the whole thing happen to her too, because I was still following the advice that wrecked my own heel.

I'm done being polite about this. If your heel hurts and you're in a Facebook group right now asking whether to get a second shot or which orthotics to buy next, you are wasting time and money your feet don't have.

Read this entire post. Every word. Because the answer is in here and it's not another shot.

My name is Dana Whitaker. I'm 51. I live in Louisville with my husband Steve. I've managed a Kohl's for nineteen years. Ten-hour days on a concrete floor.

My daughter Kayla is 24. She's in nursing school and waits tables on the weekends. Double shifts. Same concrete-floor life I've lived. And since she was a toddler, everyone's said the same thing: "She got your feet."

Two different women.

Same feet.

Same problem.

Mine started three years ago.

My right heel first. A sharp, stabbing pain on the first step out of bed, like stepping on a tack. Then after sitting in the office doing the schedule. Then by hour eight on the floor.

Every morning, Steve heard me on the stairs. Step. Stop. Step. Stop. One hand on the rail, one on the wall. Thirteen stairs, one at a time, like a woman twice my age. He used to joke about it. Then he stopped joking.

I went to a podiatrist.

"Plantar fasciitis. Very common in people on their feet all day. Let's give you a cortisone shot."

$250. But it worked.

For seven weeks it was a miracle. No tack in the morning. I came down the stairs like a normal person. I did a full Black Friday shift, fourteen hours, and drove home without my heel throbbing on the gas pedal.

I thought we were done.

Then it started coming back.

Not all at once. Slowly. Like someone turning up the volume one notch at a time.

A little ache after a long shift. A little tack in the morning. Then step, stop, step on the stairs again. Faint at first. Then every morning.

I went back.

"Let's do another one."

The second shot lasted four weeks.

"Let's get you into custom orthotics too."

$450. On top of the shots. On top of the night splint he'd put me in the month before.

The third shot lasted ten days.

"We can only do three a year in the same spot. Let's add physical therapy."

$40 a copay, twice a week.

And I was still limping. Still coming down the stairs one at a time. Still sitting in my car in the Kohl's lot for five minutes after every shift before I could make myself push the gas pedal.

I posted in a plantar fasciitis Facebook group.

"Three cortisone shots, orthotics, PT, still in pain. Has anyone dealt with this?"

Everyone had suggestions.

"You need Hokas. Changed my life."

"Oofos in the house. Never go barefoot."

"Freeze a water bottle and roll it every night."

"Compression sleeves at work."

"Roll a golf ball under your foot at your desk."

"Toe-spacer socks."

So I tried. I tried everything they told me to try.

Hokas. Two pairs, $300. Felt nice. Still limped.

Oofos for the house. $60. Still the tack in the morning.

The frozen water bottle every night in front of the TV for a year. My foot was numb for twenty minutes. Then it wasn't.

Compression sleeves. A golf ball in my desk drawer. Toe socks. A $90 massage gun.

I stopped adding up the total because the number made me physically sick.

And my heel was getting worse.

By year three, I wasn't just limping in the mornings. I was limping all day. I'd started walking on the outside edge of my right foot, and now my knee hurt, and my hip hurt on that side too.

I stopped walking the dog. Steve took over. I stopped going to my nephew's baseball games because the bleachers were too far from the parking lot. I stopped walking the floor at work and started managing from the office, which isn't how I've ever managed.

I started looking tired. Not just tired. Defeated. Like I'd accepted that this was my body now.

Steve said that look is what scared him.

In March, my podiatrist said the word "surgery" for the first time.

I went home and printed out the transfer paperwork for a desk job at the district office. A pay cut. No more store. No more floor. No more team I'd built for nineteen years.

I'm not proud of that.

I took the paperwork into the stockroom on my break the next day and sat down on a box of returns and read it, and I cried. Not quietly.

Kayla was working a shift at the store that week, filling in during spring break. She found me back there. She didn't say anything. She just went and got a bag of ice from the break room freezer and sat down on the floor next to me and held it on my heel.

My daughter, taking care of me in a stockroom.

I wanted to scream.

That was a Tuesday. I remember, because the next Saturday Kayla came home from a double shift at the restaurant, sat down on the bottom stair, and said:

"Mom, my heel's been killing me in the mornings."

She was 24. Waiting tables on concrete. Same feet.

I knew it immediately. The same first-step pain. The same heel. The same life.

I knew what was coming. I'd lived the entire three years. I knew exactly what the next three years looked like for her.

Three years of shots that work and then fade. Three years of shoes and inserts that change nothing. Three years of advice aimed at the wrong target. Three years of bills while the problem gets worse underneath.

I could not watch her do it.

I couldn't spend another $6,000. I couldn't watch my daughter come down the stairs one step at a time at 24. I couldn't sit in another stockroom and cry.

I needed to understand why.

Not what to try next. Why.

Why did the shot work and then stop. Why did each one wear off faster than the last. Why did every shoe and insert change nothing. Why did it keep getting worse no matter what I threw at it.

Three podiatrists and two physical therapists in three years. Not one of them answered why. They all answered what. What to inject. What to wear. What to stretch.

Not one of them told me why everything kept failing.

I spent two weeks reading. Every night after Steve went to bed. Reddit. Facebook groups. Medical articles I had to read three times.

And at 2 AM on a Tuesday I found a post from a woman whose physical therapist, one who works with runners, had explained something to her that nobody had ever explained to me.

And when I read it, I felt the floor drop out from under me.

Because it explained everything.

Why the shot works and then fades. Why each one wears off faster. Why the shoes and inserts don't fix anything. Why it gets worse every year no matter what you do.

And it was so simple, so obvious once someone says it, that I wanted to throw my phone across the room.

Here's what nobody told me for three years.

Your plantar fascia is made of collagen. Type I collagen, almost entirely. It's a thick band along the bottom of your foot that takes your whole body weight with every step.

Every step wears it down a tiny bit. And every day, your body is supposed to rebuild that wear with new, strong collagen.

But your body makes less collagen every year after your mid-twenties. And when it can't keep up, it patches the wear with weaker, messier tissue. Like filling a pothole with loose gravel instead of fresh asphalt. Under a microscope, chronic plantar fasciitis mostly isn't inflammation. It's degenerated, disorganized tissue. Some doctors now call it fasciosis.

That's the tack in the morning. That's the pain after sitting. That's the ache at hour eight. All of it. One band of tissue wearing out faster than it's being rebuilt.

Cortisone doesn't rebuild anything. It shuts down the pain and the body's reaction to the damage. That's all it does. It doesn't touch the tissue. The tissue keeps wearing out while the shot hides it.

That's why it works for seven weeks and then fades. It's not that the shot stopped working. It's that the damage underneath kept growing while the shot hid it. The shot was losing a race against a pothole that keeps getting bigger.

So you get another shot. It helps for a bit. The pothole gets worse. So you add orthotics. They help for a bit. The pothole gets worse. So the shots wear off faster. Seven weeks. Then four. Then ten days.

More paint over the hole. Bigger hole. The paint can't keep up. It never will.

And it gets worse.

That physical therapist told the woman something else. Research suggests cortisone actually slows down the cells that make new collagen. And repeated shots are linked to the fascia thinning and even tearing, and to the fat pad under the heel wasting away.

So the shots I was paying $250 for weren't just losing the race against my heel.

They may have been helping it break down faster.

For three years.

Three years. Three podiatrists. Two PTs. Three shots. A shockwave session. Orthotics. Night splint. Hokas. Oofos. Ice. Sleeves. Golf ball. $6,000 and counting.

And the tissue got worse through all of it.

Because not one person told me about the tissue. Not once in three years did anyone say the word collagen to me. Not one podiatrist. Not one PT. Not one Facebook group. Nobody.

They told me what to buy. They never told me why it wouldn't work.

The why is the tissue.

The next morning I called every physical therapist within 40 miles who worked with runners. Found one who'd see me that week. Drove 35 minutes. Didn't care.

She was the first person in three years who didn't recommend a shot.

She confirmed everything I'd read at 2 AM. The collagen. The weak patching. The shot losing the race. The shot possibly speeding it up.

All of it.

Then she said the thing that made everything click.

"Your fascia needs its building materials to rebuild. Collagen. The actual protein it's made of. You can't rebuild a collagen band with cortisone. You can't rebuild it with orthotics or ice or better shoes. None of those things are collagen. Your body needs collagen, and it needs vitamin C to build with it."

"So I just buy collagen?"

"Not that simple. What's in your cabinet right now?"

I'd brought a bag, because I'd had a feeling she'd ask. Everything I'd bought over three years that had "collagen" or "joint" on the label. Six bottles and tubs.

She turned each one over and read the back out loud.

"This one's a beauty blend. Types I and III, dosed for skin. No vitamin C."

"These capsules are 750 milligrams for two. The studies on tendons used 5 to 15 grams a day. You'd need fourteen pills."

"Gummies. About a gram, plus sugar."

"This 'joint' one is type II collagen. That's cartilage collagen. It's for knees. Your fascia is type I."

"This is just turmeric. It might calm things down. It gives your fascia nothing to rebuild with."

Don't stop anything else. Keep the orthotics and the stretches. Just add the scoop and the walk, and let the tissue rebuild underneath."
